title: sleep
hook: a stool stands on three legs; the Charaka Samhita says a life does too, and one of them is sleep

segments.voice: Last week ended with food as practice and the Chandogya's chain: pure intake, a clear inner being, every knot loosened.

A milking stool has three legs, and there's a reason. On a rough barn floor, three legs always find their footing. Pull one away, though, and the whole thing tips. The Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, describes a human life the same way, propped up by three supports. We've just spent our days on the first of them, food. The second is easily treated as empty space between the parts of the day that count. Today we start on sleep.
screen: `A STOOL ON THREE LEGS.` → `PULL ONE, IT TIPS.` → `THE SECOND SUPPORT.`

segments.voice: Charaka's word is upastambha, a support or prop, the kind that keeps something standing. He names three for life: food, sleep, and brahmacharya, which here means a disciplined, restrained way of living, especially around desire. Held well, he says, these three keep a body endowed with strength, good color and growth. Then, in a later chapter, a large claim about sleep. Paraphrased: happiness and unhappiness, strength and weakness, knowing and not knowing, even life itself, depend on sleep, on whether it's taken rightly or wrongly. That's a lot to hang on something done with the eyes closed. Three things follow. First, sleep isn't time off from the practice. It's one of the legs the practice stands on. A morning routine, a careful meal, a quiet sit: all of them lean on the night before. Second, happiness and knowing are on the list, so sleep reaches into the mind as well as the body. Third, rightly or wrongly. The text doesn't praise sleep as such. It speaks of sleep in the right measure and at the right time, and warns that too much, too little or the wrong hour does harm. And said plainly: the classical texts offer a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Sleep trouble that lasts, snoring that stops and starts, or exhaustion that won't lift: those go to a doctor. What Charaka adds to an ordinary evening is a change of rank. Sleep stops being leftover time, and becomes a support.
screen: `UPASTAMBHA: A SUPPORT` · `FOOD, SLEEP, A DISCIPLINED LIFE` · `HAPPINESS AND KNOWING HANG ON IT` · `RIGHT MEASURE, RIGHT TIME`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down and notice what's under you, a chair, a floor, a bed, letting your weight go into it a little more with each breath out: shoulders, arms, hands, back, legs, all the way to the heels. Nothing to fall asleep to; just the feeling of being held up by something that isn't you. If you pray, give thanks for the last night of rest you had.
Sleep. Nidra, in Sanskrit. For Charaka, one of three supports of life, with food and a disciplined way of living. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Food, sleep and a disciplined life: three legs, and the stool stands. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: In Ayurveda's classical routine, sleep at a regular hour belongs to the round of the day and night, and the texts count it among the three supports of life.

chat.meaning: For Charaka, sleep is an upastambha, a support of life with food and brahmacharya; happiness, strength and knowing depend on taking it rightly.

notes: First day of the sleep block. Confirm the three upastambhas at Sutrasthana 11.35 (Charaka uses svapna/nidra for sleep) and the gloss of brahmacharya as 'a disciplined, restrained way of living, especially around desire'.
Sutrasthana 21 (verse numbers approximate, around 21.36): the list of things that depend on sleep. The lesson softens 'life and death' to 'even life itself'; confirm.
'Steady, strong and bright' is a loose paraphrase of Charaka's benefits of the three supports (strength, complexion, growth); confirm.
Science-seat line: lasting sleep trouble, interrupted snoring, unexplained exhaustion go to a doctor. The 'short night and a short temper' line is an everyday picture, not a claim from the text.
